strengths: Novel integration of consistency models (CMs) as proximal operators within a Plug-and-Play ADMM framework, enabling efficient inverse problem solving with as few as 2-4 neural function evaluations (NFEs).
Provides a theoretical guarantee (Theorem 1) showing that noise injection preserves the convergence of PnP-ADMM under diminishing noise, with a detailed proof in Appendix A.

Comprehensive experiments across multiple inverse problems (inpainting, super-resolution, Gaussian deblurring, and MRI reconstruction) demonstrating state-of-the-art performance in few NFEs, including the first CM trained for MRI datasets.
Ablation studies clearly validate the individual contributions of momentum and noise injection to reconstruction quality.
Clear presentation with a complete algorithm, implementation details, and extensive additional results in the appendix, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation for natural images is limited to the LSUN Bedroom dataset, which may restrict generalization to more diverse image domains; the authors acknowledge this limitation.

The theoretical convergence guarantee is only established for noise injection; the Nesterov momentum component lacks a formal proof, yet the abstract and introduction imply that the full algorithm maintains the baseline convergence properties.
For MRI reconstruction, comparisons are limited to DPS and DDS (CM4IR fails in this setting), leaving a gap in benchmarking against other CM-based or optimization-based MRI solvers.
The claim that the method 'maintains the convergence properties' may be slightly overstated given that momentum coefficients are tuned heuristically without theoretical guarantees.

strengths: Elegant and original framing: reinterpreting consistency models (CMs) as proximal operators of a learned prior so they can be plugged directly into a PnP-ADMM solver. This is a clean conceptual bridge between the CM and PnP-optimization literatures and is more principled than the pseudo-inverse/back-projection guidance used by CM4IR or the ControlNet retraining used by CoSIGN.

Strong practical efficiency claims that are actually supported: PnP-CM matches or beats DPS (1000 NFE), DDS (100 NFE), CM (40 NFE), CoSIGN (4 NFE), and CM4IR (4 NFE) using only 2-4 NFE. Table 1 shows clear wins on inpainting (27.95 PSNR / 0.219 LPIPS vs. CM4IR 26.78 / 0.303) and Gaussian deblurring (28.10 / 0.237 vs. 27.37 / 0.270), and Table 2 shows a substantial margin on Coronal PD and PD-FS MRI at both R=4 and R=8 (e.g., 32.69 PSNR vs. 31.93 DDS and 31.21 DPS at R=4).

The theoretical additions are non-trivial: Theorem 1 (with the proof in Appendix A) gives a Lipschitz-based bound on the residual introduced by noise injection and states the summability condition (Σ‖η_k‖₂ < ∞) under which the baseline PnP-ADMM convergence is preserved. This is a meaningful formalization of a heuristic that is widely used but rarely justified.

First consistency model trained specifically for MRI, plus the use of the NYU fastMRI knee dataset with the standard slice-exclusion protocol (10 validation volumes, 228 PD / 240 PD-FS slices). This is a useful, reproducible medical-imaging contribution and the qualitative figures (Figs. 3 and 7) show that PnP-CM removes the aliasing/structured artifacts that DPS and DDS leave behind.

Good empirical hygiene: an ablation (Table 3) isolating the contributions of momentum and noise injection, an extended noise-level/NFE table (Table 4), and implementation details for all baselines (Appendix B) including re-tuning DPS likelihood weights for the new datasets and training CoSIGN ControlNets from scratch where checkpoints were unavailable.
weaknesses: Natural-image evaluation is confined to a single dataset (LSUN Bedroom), which the authors themselves flag as a limitation. Because the CM was pre-trained on that same dataset, the natural-image results are somewhat in-distribution, and the generality of the method relative to CM4IR/CoSIGN is not established on a second domain (e.g., ImageNet, FFHQ).

Gains over the closest CM-based competitor are mixed rather than decisive on super-resolution: at 4 NFE, PnP-CM (25.63 PSNR / 0.322 LPIPS) is essentially tied with CM4IR (25.60 / 0.320), with LPIPS actually slightly worse. The headline "state-of-the-art" claim rests mainly on the deblurring, inpainting, and MRI settings, and the paper would benefit from a more careful characterization of when the ADMM framing helps versus when it does not.

The theoretical guarantees are weaker than the text implies. Theorem 1 assumes a diminishing, summable noise sequence, but the actual method runs for only 2-4 outer iterations with a fine-tuned fixed noise level, so the regime in which the proof applies is not the regime in which the method is used. Similarly, the Nesterov-momentum convergence guarantee is asserted by citing restart-scheme theory but the paper states that coefficients are "fine-tuned heuristically," so the practical algorithm is not covered by the cited convergence results.

Hyperparameters (penalty parameters, momentum coefficients, injected noise level) are independently fine-tuned per task and per NFE budget. This raises the concern that part of the reported advantage over baselines comes from tuning effort rather than from the algorithmic contribution; a sensitivity study or a single shared hyperparameter setting would strengthen the claim.

The step-3 data-fidelity solve uses SVD for small problems and CG for large-scale MRI, meaning the exact proximal update of Eq. 10 is only approximated in the large-scale regime. The interaction between CG tolerance and the ADMM convergence argument (and the noise-injection bound) is not discussed, and could matter for the MRI results where the solver is only approximately applied.

CM4IR is reported to "fail" on multi-coil MRI because its back-projection fidelity A^†(y−Ax) becomes aliased when m > n. This is a predictable consequence of CM4IR's design rather than an empirical surprise, so the comparison is somewhat asymmetric; a fairer test would include an adapted CM4IR variant or clearly separate the failure-mode analysis from the accuracy comparison.

strengths: The central idea of reinterpreting consistency models as proximal operators inside a plug-and-play ADMM scheme is a reasonable and moderately novel framing that connects two otherwise separate lines of work (CM-based inverse solvers and PnP optimization).

Because ADMM's data-fidelity subproblem is quadratically regularized (Eq. 10), the method can exploit conjugate gradients rather than a back-projection/PGD update, which is a legitimate and well-motivated advantage over CM4IR-style pseudo-inverse fidelity in ill-conditioned settings.

Training a consistency model from scratch for MRI (fastMRI) and reporting it as a first-of-its-kind result is a useful, if incremental, contribution, and the MRI results (Table 2) show non-trivial gains over DPS (1000 NFE) and DDS (100 NFE).
The paper is generally well-organized, the algorithm (Alg. 1) is clearly presented, and the qualitative figures across four tasks are informative.
Theorem 1 provides at least a formal statement that controlled diminishing noise injection does not destroy the fixed-point behavior of the baseline, which is a sensible addition.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited. PnP-ADMM with a deep denoiser as the proximal operator is long-established (Chan et al. 2016; Venkatakrishnan et al. 2013), and the actual new ingredients here—substituting a CM, adding Nesterov momentum, and injecting noise—are standard, generic techniques. The paper reads largely as a competent engineering combination rather than a conceptual advance.

The efficiency claim is misleading. '4 NFEs' counts only neural-network evaluations and ignores the cost of the data-fidelity update, which is solved by SVD/CG (Sec. B) and can require many forward/adjoint applications per outer iteration, especially for multi-coil MRI. No wall-clock or FLOP comparison is reported anywhere, despite efficiency being a headline claim. The NFE comparison against DPS/DDS is therefore not apples-to-apples.

The quantitative gains over the closest baseline (CM4IR) are marginal: for SR×4 at 4 NFE, PSNR is 25.63 vs. 25.60 (0.03 dB, clearly within noise), and the abstract's claim of 'consistently outperforming comparable CM-based approaches' overstates the evidence. Only LPIPS shows a consistent margin.

The ablation (Table 3) undercuts a core claimed contribution: noise injection alone barely helps (e.g., deblurring 27.46→27.58, SR 20.95→20.83, i.e. worse), and the gain is almost entirely attributable to momentum (28.05 with momentum only vs. 28.10 with both). The near-zero practical benefit of noise injection also makes Theorem 1 largely decorative.

Theorem 1 is a routine Lipschitz perturbation bound and is weak in two respects: it assumes the baseline PnP-ADMM converges to a fixed point, which is not guaranteed for a general (non-nonexpansive) CM denoiser, and the required condition (diminishing noise with finite sum) is trivially satisfiable, so the 'maintains convergence guarantees' statement is thin. Moreover, momentum—arguably the more important accelerator—is explicitly heuristic with no guarantee, contradicting the abstract's framing that the method 'maintains the convergence properties of the baseline PnP-ADMM.'

The evaluation breadth is very narrow for the natural-image setting: only LSUN Bedroom (a single, low-diversity bedroom dataset), which the authors themselves flag as a limitation. There is no ImageNet/FFHQ evaluation, so generalizability claims rest on one domain. The DM-based comparison is also thin (only DPS for natural images), omitting many recent fast diffusion solvers.

Baseline treatment is uneven and likely unfair. CoSIGN is retrained from scratch for inpainting and deblurring (no checkpoints available), whereas PnP-CM uses pre-trained CMs and per-task tuning; CM (Song et al.) is an unconditional model not designed as an inverse solver, so its 40-NFE numbers are not a meaningful 'comparable CM-based' reference. These choices inflate the apparent margins.

The method requires independent per-task tuning of the injected noise level and the primal/dual momentum coefficients (Sec. 4.3, App. B), with no principled selection rule. This raises fairness and reproducibility concerns and suggests the approach is not robust out-of-the-box in the few-step regime it targets.

Applicability is restricted to linear forward operators. The closed-form z-update in Eq. 10 and the CG solver depend on a linear A, and nonlinear operators are deferred to future work. This limits the 'plug-and-play' generality claimed in the title and abstract.

Several claims in the abstract/introduction are stronger than what is demonstrated: e.g., 'state-of-the-art' results and 'meaningful outputs in just two steps' are supported only by PSNR/LPIPS on one natural dataset plus SSIM/PSNR for MRI, with no perceptual metrics for MRI and no runtime evidence for the efficiency story.

strengths: Novel and sensible framing: reinterpreting consistency models (CMs) as proximal operators of a prior allows their seamless integration into established plug-and-play (PnP)/ADMM optimization, combining CM sampling efficiency with PnP's optimization structure.

Strong empirical efficiency: PnP-CM achieves competitive or state-of-the-art reconstruction quality among CM-based methods with only 4 NFEs (and 2 steps in some tasks), a meaningful practical improvement over DM-based solvers requiring 1000 NFEs.

Broad evaluation spanning linear (super-resolution, Gaussian deblurring, inpainting), nonlinear (JPEG restoration, nonlinear deblurring, phase retrieval), and medical imaging (fastMRI knee reconstruction with PD and PD-FS contrasts) tasks, plus two natural-image datasets (CelebA-HQ, LSUN Bedroom).
First application of a CM trained specifically on MRI data (fastMRI), with consistent gains over DPS, DDS, and CM4IR on PSNR/SSIM at R=4 and R=8.
Reasonable theoretical grounding: Theorem 1 provides a perturbation bound showing that bounded, diminishing noise injection preserves ADMM fixed-point convergence (proof in SuppMat A).

Ablation study (Table 2) cleanly disentangles the contributions of momentum and noise injection, and SuppMat D.2 provides a hyperparameter sensitivity analysis showing robustness to ±25% perturbations.
Reproducibility is well-supported: detailed hyperparameter tables, comparison-method tuning procedures, and training details for DM and CM networks are provided in the supplementary material.
weaknesses: The core novelty is somewhat incremental: PnP-ADMM with a deep denoiser is well established (PnP-DM, DiffPIR, etc.), and the specific acceleration devices (noise injection and momentum in ADMM) are adapted from prior work (CM4IR, Deng et al.). The 'CM as proximal operator' observation is arguably a relabeling of using the CM as a denoiser, rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Theorem 1 is a relatively shallow Lipschitz-based perturbation argument and only addresses noise injection; the momentum modification is not covered by the analysis, yet the paper claims to 'preserve convergence guarantees' generally. The claim of preserved guarantees is thus only partially justified.

The practical benefit of the quadratic ADMM penalty over preconditioned gradient descent is asserted (better conditioning) but not empirically isolated; the paper states ADMM 'requires fewer iterations' without a direct experimental comparison to a PGD-based CM solver.

Comparison fairness: the strongest DM baselines (DPS, DPnP, DiffPIR) operate at 1000-2923 NFEs while PnP-CM runs at 4, which is a somewhat lopsided comparison; the most relevant baselines are CM4IR and CoSIGN, and gains over them are more modest (e.g., nonlinear deblurring LPIPS 0.304 vs 0.297 for CM4IR on CelebA-HQ).

Some tasks are not compared against all baselines (e.g., phase retrieval omits IIGDM and DPnP; the table shows '4 or 8' NFEs for PnP-CM nonlinear tasks, and the NFE reporting is inconsistent across rows).
Evaluation is restricted to 256×256 images and specific datasets; scalability to higher resolutions or larger-scale inverse problems—one of the paper's stated motivations—is not demonstrated.

No wall-clock or memory comparisons are provided; the headline claim of efficiency rests solely on NFE counts, which do not directly reflect practical runtime given the SVD/CG computations for the data-fidelity step.

strengths: Conceptually clean and useful reframing: interpreting consistency models (CMs) as proximal operators of a prior (Sec. 3.1) lets an efficient few-step generator be dropped into a standard PnP/ADMM solver, combining CM sampling efficiency with the convergence machinery of PnP. This is a more principled integration than the task-specific ControlNet (CoSIGN) or pseudo-inverse (CM4IR) alternatives.

Strong and broad empirical evidence at very low compute. Table 1 shows PnP-CM (4 NFEs, 8 for phase retrieval) attaining the best PSNR on nearly every linear and nonlinear task (SRx4, Gaussian deblurring, inpainting, JPEG, nonlinear deblurring, phase retrieval) against DPS (1000 NFE), DiffPIR (100), DnP (2923), PnP-DM (2034), CM (40), CoSIGN (4), and CM4IR (4), with qualitative corroboration in Figs. 2-3 and the supplement (Figs. 6-11).

Genuine extension to a hard, practical setting: training a CM on fastMRI and applying it to multi-coil MRI reconstruction (Sec. 4.1-4.3). PnP-CM outperforms DPS, DDS, and CM4IR on both Coronal PD and PD-FS at R=4 and R=8 in PSNR/SSIM (Table 1, Fig. 4, Fig. 12), which is a meaningful medical-imaging contribution rather than a toy benchmark.

The nonlinear inverse-problem results are a real differentiator: the ADMM quadratic data-fidelity penalty makes the method robust for ill-conditioned/nonlinear operators where pseudo-inverse-based CM solvers degrade, and this is argued and demonstrated (Sec. 3.1, Table 1, Fig. 3).

Reasonable theoretical and empirical diligence around the proposed accelerations: Theorem 1 (proof in Supp. A) bounds the divergence introduced by noise injection for a Lipschitz denoiser under a summable noise sequence, and the ablation in Table 2 cleanly isolates the contributions of momentum and noise injection, with momentum shown to help mainly in the low-NFE regime (Table 4).

Good reproducibility posture: complete hyperparameters (Supp. Table 3), explicit CM/EDM training details (Supp. C), baseline re-tuning descriptions (Supp. B.3), and a hyperparameter sensitivity study (Supp. Fig. 5) showing graceful degradation under +/-25% perturbation.
weaknesses: The headline claim of outperforming baselines 'in both quality and efficiency' is not fully supported by the reported metrics: on several tasks PnP-CM has worse (higher) LPIPS than competing methods, e.g. CelebA-HQ JPEG 0.356 vs DPS 0.234 and IIGDM 0.221; LSUN JPEG 0.410 vs DPS 0.285 and IIGDM 0.290; CelebA-HQ inpainting 0.201 vs DPS 0.194 and DnP 0.195; LSUN SRx4 0.321 vs DnP 0.270. The paper emphasizes PSNR in the text while these perceptual regressions are not discussed.

The technical novelty beyond the framing is modest: PnP-ADMM, the noise-injection strategy (explicitly adopted from CM4IR's schedule, Supp. B.2), and the momentum term are all taken from prior work. The main new element is the choice of CM as the denoiser/proximal operator, which is a natural composition rather than a new mechanism.

Theorem 1's guarantee is weaker than the text implies: it only shows bounded additional divergence under a diminishing, summable noise sequence (Supp. Eq. 18), i.e., a stability statement, not convergence to the same fixed point in the practical regime. Moreover, it is stated for standard PnP-ADMM while Alg. 1 uses a reverse iteration ordering and a per-iteration CM noise level delta_n; the summability assumption is asserted rather than verified for the hyperparameters in Table 3, and the result inherits any convexity/Lipschitz limitations of the baseline PnP-ADMM guarantee [12].

Phase-retrieval evaluation is potentially circular: Supp. B.1 states that among 8 valid inversions the one minimizing LPIPS to a single pre-generated unconditional CM output is selected. Since the reference is the authors' own unconditional CM sample, this selection criterion may favor PnP-CM; it is not stated whether the identical selection protocol was applied to the baseline numbers (DPS, IIGDM, DnP) in Table 1, which would be necessary for a fair comparison.

Efficiency is reported solely as NFEs; no wall-clock time, memory, or per-task compute is given despite the repeated claim of being 'significantly faster.' This matters because each PnP-CM step also runs 10 CG iterations for MRI (and SVD-based solves for linear tasks), so NFE understates the true cost relative to, e.g., CM/CoSIGN/CM4IR at the same NFE count.

Evaluation breadth and statistical rigor are limited: only two natural-image datasets and two MRI contrasts (10 validation volumes), no error bars or variance for the natural-image results, and nonlinear tasks are compared against a narrower baseline set (e.g., no CM4IR/CoSIGN for phase retrieval, where PnP-CM uses a different NFE=8 setting).

Some baseline implementations are questionable (e.g., CoSIGN's very poor LPIPS of 0.4-0.6 in Table 1, with ControlNets trained from scratch by the authors), which weakens the strength of the CM-based comparison; this is acknowledged but not remedied.

strengths: The core idea—treating a consistency model as the proximal operator/denoiser inside a plug-and-play ADMM solver—is conceptually clean and reasonably well motivated. Replacing the intractable proximal map of a learned prior with a CM denoiser is a natural extension of the PnP literature, and the paper connects it coherently to the MAP/ADMM formulation.

The empirical scope is broad: linear (SR, Gaussian deblurring, inpainting), nonlinear (JPEG restoration, nonlinear deblurring, phase retrieval), and MRI reconstruction (coronal PD and PD-FS at R=4 and R=8), with ablations on momentum and noise injection. This is a substantial amount of evaluation for one paper.
The efficiency story is legitimate: PnP-CM attains competitive PSNR at 4 NFEs, which is a real practical advantage over DPS (1000), DiffPIR (100), DnP (2923), and PnP-DM (2034).

Training a consistency model directly on fastMRI and reporting the first CM-based MRI solver is a genuine (if incremental) contribution, and the MRI results (Table 1) are consistently the strongest in that block.

Reproducibility is handled reasonably well: training details, complete hyperparameter tables, noise-schedule parameterization, and a sensitivity study are provided in the supplement, and the comparison methods follow their official implementations.
weaknesses: Novelty is thin. PnP restoration with deep denoisers is a long-established framework, and a consistency model is, by construction, a denoiser that maps a noisy sample to a clean estimate. "CMs as proximal operators" is therefore closer to a reframing than a new technical mechanism. Relative to the closest prior work (CM4IR, which also uses 4 NFEs and a CM prior), the delta is essentially ADMM instead of a pseudo-inverse PGD step—an incremental algorithmic change.

The theoretical contribution is weak. Theorem 1 only guarantees convergence under a summable injected-noise sequence (Σ‖η_k‖ < ∞). The method actually injects noise of finite, non-diminishing magnitude at every low-NFE step, so the guarantee does not describe the algorithm that is run. The proof is a routine Lipschitz perturbation bound (Eq. 15–18) and effectively says the fixed point shifts by an amount proportional to the cumulative noise.

The headline claim of "consistently outperforming existing CM-based approaches" is not supported by the tables. On inpainting, DiffPIR (100 NFEs) beats PnP-CM in both PSNR and LPIPS on CelebA-HQ (30.71/0.207 vs 29.23/0.201) and on LSUN Bedroom (28.66/0.212 vs 27.12/0.233). On the nonlinear tasks PnP-CM has markedly worse LPIPS than DPS/IIGDM (JPEG 0.356 vs 0.234/0.221; nonlinear deblur 0.304 vs 0.235), suggesting perceptually inferior reconstructions despite slightly higher PSNR. On phase retrieval it is worse than DnP (22.18/0.422 vs 22.89/0.338). The results are mixed, not uniform.

Gains over the fairest baseline (CM4IR, also 4 NFEs) are marginal and frequently within noise: LSUN SR 25.56 vs 25.50 PSNR; LSUN Gaussian deblurring 27.49 vs 27.37 PSNR (but worse LPIPS 0.285 vs 0.270); CelebA-HQ SR 27.27 vs 26.77. On MRI the reported differences carry standard deviations of similar magnitude (e.g., 35.57±1.49 vs 31.05±2.01), so the significance of the improvement is not established.

Comparing against 1000–2900 NFE solvers to claim "state-of-the-art in as few as four NFEs" is a partly unfair framing; the only apples-to-apples comparisons are at matched NFE (CM4IR/CoSIGN/CM), where the margins are small.

Several components are heuristics that undercut the generality claims: inpainting requires a median-filter initialization, and phase retrieval requires enumerating all eight inversions and selecting the one minimizing LPIPS against a pre-generated unconditional CM output—a selection step the paper itself notes adds cost and is only used at the output.

Noise injection is borrowed from CM4IR and momentum from Deng et al. (2025); the momentum coefficients are tuned per-task (Table 3), and Table 4 shows momentum's benefit is modest except in the low-NFE regime. The ablation demonstrates the components help, but they are not novel contributions of this work.
